title: The Funhe verses

cards: Har haan. Two syllables, like a foot coming down at the turn of a dance step. Har haan.
Right after the Gatha, on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-one, come Guru Arjan's Funhe, short verses that each turn on that same small refrain. Yesterday was density, one line folded tight.
Today is rhythm, the same beat returning verse after verse, the way a heart keeps time. And what that heart keeps time for, it turns out, is someone it misses.

teach.b: The Funhe are short rhythmic verses of longing, and both halves matter. First, the rhythm.
In each verse, the last line opens with har haan, a refrain some explain as the Lord's name with a sung affirmation, something like yes, Lord.
Because it comes back every time, the verses have a pulse you can feel before you follow the meaning. Then, the longing.
They open with an image, paraphrased: with pen in hand, the Inaccessible One writes on the forehead.
From there the verses keep reaching toward the Beloved: the Lord's beauty, the wish to meet, the sweetness of the holy company where the Name is sung.
They're short enough that the longing never becomes a speech. It just keeps arriving, beat by beat. Why would longing want a rhythm?
Missing someone works like this. It doesn't come once and leave. It comes back on its own schedule: at the kettle, at the door, at the same hour each night.
The Funhe give that returning a shape and a direction.

Instead of a wound that reopens, the return becomes a refrain, a place the heart keeps landing on purpose. Seen this way, a repeating line in kirtan isn't filler. It's the heart finding its footing, again.

how: Guru Arjan's Funhe are read as part of the closing sections of the Guru Granth Sahib, and some are sung in kirtan, where the refrain har haan gives the singing its pulse.

games.q: a missing keeps coming back to you, at the same hour each night. what do the Funhe do with a feeling like that?
o: argue it away with a long speech.
give it a rhythm, so the return becomes a refrain.
games.why: the Funhe let longing keep arriving, beat by beat, each time landing on har haan.

practice: If you can find the Funhe on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-one, read three of them slowly, and let your voice drop a little on every har haan, like a step landing.
If not, let the breath be the rhythm: in, and on the out-breath, the two syllables, quietly, har haan. Don't force a feeling; just let the beat come back, and notice what it reaches for.
